title: the Manusmriti — read critically
tomorrow: Priya has to pick one text to read critically for class. which?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kalki and the sandal-scented breeze: the hinge where the age of truth comes round again, and the end of the Puranas. Today, a different kind of book.
screen: `THE AGE OF TRUTH COMES ROUND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: A guy in Priya's comments keeps quoting the same old book at her, verse numbers and all, as if that settles every argument: it's in the Hindu rulebook. The book is the Manusmriti, the laws of Manu. It's real, it's old, and some of it is hard to read. But is it the Hindu rulebook? The book itself points somewhere else first. So today's question: what do you do with an old book that says hard things?
screen: `'IT'S IN THE HINDU RULEBOOK.'` → `REAL, OLD, AND HARD TO READ.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH IT?`

segments.voice: Start with what it is: a dharma text in verse, on duties, marriage, kings, food, purity and punishment. The tradition calls it smriti, and Manu itself says the Veda is shruti and books like this one are smriti, set beside it. Now the hard part, said plainly. It ranks people by the family they're born into and sets harsher rules for those lower down, and some of its verses limit women's freedom. Some Hindus, reformers among them, have challenged it hard, and some reject it outright. Here's the tradition's own answer, from inside the book. In its second chapter, Manu names where dharma comes from: the Veda first, then tradition, then the conduct of good people, and last, what sits right with one's own self. So even this law book doesn't ask to be read alone. It gives a reader four places to stand, and one of them is conscience. A neighbor tradition knows this problem well. The Torah says, "eye for eye, tooth for tooth." The rabbis of the Talmud read it as payment for the injury, not a matching wound. That's the shared thing: a hard line in an old law, read by a later community with care, not just repeated. And the honest difference: in Jewish tradition, the rabbis' reading became part of the law itself. Hindu tradition has no single court for Manu; teachers and families keep, reshape or set aside its rules in different ways. Read it whole. Say what it says. Then weigh it.
screen: `SMRITI, SET BESIDE THE VEDA.` · `IT RANKS BY BIRTH. SOME PUSH BACK.` · `FOUR SOURCES, AND ONE IS CONSCIENCE.` · `EYE FOR EYE, READ AS PAYMENT.` · then, large: `READ IT WHOLE. SAY WHAT IT SAYS.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write two short lines: one rule you grew up with that you keep, and one you've questioned. Set them side by side and look at both for the sit, breathing slowly. Nothing needs deciding yet.
The Manusmriti: the laws of Manu, an old dharma text in verse; a smriti, set beside the Veda, with hard verses and its own list of where dharma comes from.
Your line: the Manusmriti, read critically. Read it whole, say what it says, and let conscience have its say too. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus relate to the Manusmriti in different ways: some cite parts of it, many teachers read it alongside other dharma texts and the Veda, and some Hindus, reformers among them, reject it.

fork.setup: your club's old rulebook has one rule that's plainly unfair. a member says: obey every line or ignore the whole thing. what does today's reading suggest?
options: read it all, name the unfair rule honestly, and weigh it against the rest.
obey every line exactly; a rulebook only works if nobody questions it.
skip it entirely; an old rulebook can't teach anyone anything now.
fork.reveal: reading critically isn't obeying every line or never opening the book: Manu's own list sets the Veda, good people's conduct and one's own self beside its rules.

chat.says: a guy online keeps quoting Manu at me like it's THE Hindu rulebook. is it, though??
options: no. it's smriti, set beside the Veda, and it even lists conscience as a source.
yes. every Hindu follows it as law, so he's quoting the actual rulebook.
no, because it's fake; those verses he quotes aren't really in it at all.
chat.meaning: The Manusmriti is smriti. It names the Veda as dharma's first source, then tradition, good people's conduct, and what sits right with one's own self.

notes: First day of 'the Manusmriti — read critically' (The dharma texts, 1567 on). Angle: what the book is, the hard parts named plainly, and the book's own list of the sources of dharma as a tool for critical reading. 1569 (another writer) takes apaddharma and the chandala; 1570 takes 'honors women and limits them', so this day names the women's verses only in one clause.
Keeper question from the outline is still open: 'read critically or not at all?' This day reads it critically and does not present its rankings as the tradition's settled view.

UNITY THREAD (wisdom day): shared with Judaism = a hard line in an old law read by a later community with care (Exodus 21:24, JPS 1917; Talmud Bava Kamma 83b–84a reads it as compensation). Honest difference = in Jewish tradition the rabbinic reading became law (halakha); Hindu tradition has no single court for Manu. Jewish law is not used as a foil; neither tradition ranked. Ask a Jewish reader to check the one-line summary.

Manu 2.6 / 2.12 paraphrased; 'what sits right with one's own self' renders atmatushti (Bühler: 'self-satisfaction'; 'one's own pleasure'); 'conscience' in the voice is an interpretive gloss; confirm it is fair. Manu 2.10 paraphrased (shruti = Veda; smriti = dharmashastra).

'Some Hindus, reformers among them, have challenged it hard, and some reject it outright' is general on purpose (B. R. Ambedkar's public burning of the text is the best-known case; the next writer's run plans Ambedkar). No date or number given under the claims rule.
'Hindu tradition has no single court for Manu' is a summary, not a cited claim; confirm phrasing.
